questions.q: $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. Which value of $P(A \cap B)$ is actually possible?
questions.explain: The overlap is boxed in: $\max(0, P(A)+P(B)-1) \le P(A \cap B) \le \min(P(A), P(B))$, i.e. $[0.2, 0.5]$. $0.1$ would make $P(A \cup B) = 1.1 > 1$; $0.6$ and $0.75$ exceed $P(B)$ — the overlap can't be bigger than either event.

questions.q: $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. Which statement is true?
options: They are independent, since one doesn't affect the other
$P(A \mid B) = 0 \ne P(A)$, so they are dependent
questions.explain: Disjoint means $P(A \cap B) = 0$, so $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$ and $P(A \mid B) = 0$: learning B happened rules A out — strong dependence. The $0.12$ options wrongly apply the independence product rule.

questions.q: You run 10 independent significance tests at $\alpha = 0.05$, and in truth nothing is going on. What is the probability of **at least one** false positive?
questions.explain: Complement trick: $P(\text{none}) = 0.95^{10} \approx 0.599$, so $P(\ge 1) = 1 - 0.599 \approx 0.401$. $10 \times 0.05$ is the union bound — an upper limit, not the exact value — and $0.95^{10}$ is the probability of *no* false positive.

De Morgan: $A^c \cap B^c = (A \cup B)^c$, so $P = 1 - (0.3 + 0.2 - 0.1) = 0.6$. $0.56 = 0.7 \times 0.8$ assumes independence, $0.5$ forgets the overlap, and $0.9 = 1 - P(A \cap B)$ is $P(A^c \cup B^c)$ — the other law.
